title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
snippet: According to Elorian's evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.
fullText:
Elorian, the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.

The model, Glimpse, is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see. 

Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw.

For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night. 

Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.”

“Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said. 

The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against. 

Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna.

But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks. 

Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean.

The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media, and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. That means building a model of a scene using that to choose an action, including directly controlling robots. Next year, Dai said, the company aims to build “the world’s best visual reasoning model,” one that leads on every visual reasoning test.

title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
snippet: The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles.
fullText:
AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” 

The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.”

This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.

At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.

Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers.

CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information.

For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords.

In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.

title: Voicemod’s New Phone Gadget Changes Your ‘Sonic Identity’ for Mobile Games and Streaming
snippet: Clip it to the back of your phone, and it’ll convert your voice on the fly for fun, privacy and accessibility.
fullText:
For years, Voicemod has given people a way to change their voices online, which they’ve done for any number of benign reasons — for game players with feminine-pitched voices to avoid harassment, for those with damaged vocal cords to simulate their former voices, for anonymity or even just for fun. Now the company has a new product to bring its voice-changing tech on the go in a physical device that magnetically clips on the back of phones.

The Voicemod Key Pocket, available to preorder now for $130, is a small soundboard about the size of a magnetic battery and serves as a controller interface for the company’s voice-changing apps. The half-dozen buttons on the back of the device can be used to switch between voices or audio effects while streaming or playing games, while the wheel adjusts volume of the projected voice. 

The Key Pocket works in tandem with the Voicemod app, but all voice processing is done locally and in real time separate from games and streaming apps in order to maximize privacy as well as performance, according to a Voicemod statement. The Voicemod app provides access to over 200 original voices made by the company, over 76,000 voices made by the service’s community and over 800,000 sounds and memes made by users. 

			

More from CNET

The Key Pocket is a versatile gizmo, with an LED wheel at the top-left corner for toggling voices and checking sound setup, while programmable trigger buttons enable swapping between voices and soundboard playback. The device supports wired and Bluetooth wireless headsets, has USB passthrough charging and clips securely to the back of phones with MagSafe-compatible magnets. 

Beyond phones, the Key Pocket works on tablets and consoles, including PS4 and PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2 and the Meta Quest 2, 3 and 3S headsets. It can plug into USB-C, wired 3.5mm ports or connect via Bluetooth.

There are plenty of reasons folks might want to change their voice, from goofing off with friends to avoiding harassment when gaming online — a sad reality for gamers with feminine voices. It’s also an accessibility boon for people who have health conditions or other circumstances leading them to want to change their vocal timbre and pitch.

These days, changing voices can be cause for concern, especially with artificial-intelligence scams spoofing the voices of loved ones to extort money. But when I sat down at Mobile World Congress 2026 earlier this year to chat with Voicemod’s Daniel Pearson, vice president of marketing, and Alex Bordanova, chief product and technology officer, they explained how it aligned with the ethos of the company. The Key Pocket is the result of years of Voicemod’s work to support the idea that one’s online voice is as much an expression of identity as their visual look.

“Everyone has their digital visual appearance where they tweak their cosmetics and skins, but when it comes to voice, it’s kind of been left out, right? It’s this missing half of digital identity,” said Pearson. 

As voice-changing tech makes its way into Fortnite, Arc Raiders, Marvel Rivals and other spaces for online third spaces, people are opening up to the idea that their personal expression isn’t just limited to how they’re seen, but also how they’re heard — or as Pearson calls it, their “sonic identity.”

Voicemod

When voice becomes a way to express identity

In our earlier chat, Pearson and Bordanova laid out what Voicemod meant to its community, with the latter describing one memorable story from last October’s TwitchCon 2025. A woman approached him explaining that she was a streamer who lost her voice for about six months but was able to make up for it with Voicemod’s tech.

“She used an AI voice, because that was enough to turn something audible out of just very nuanced sounds that she could project,” Bordanova said. 

It spurred discussion about ways the Voicemod team might preserve the community’s voices — a vault, say, to future-proof their voices in the event that health or injury might limit their speaking. 

The Voicemod creators don’t just see its tech as just to alter voices for fun or privacy — they see it as an expression machine, one that reflects who you are online. That comes in the form of a voice tweaked to a desired pitch and timbre, but also more abstract communication, like a soundboard. Yes, the signature toy of radio shock jocks from yesteryear is an aspect of expression, too, especially among a community where sounds take on specific meanings.

“It’s giving you the capacity to react and expand by giving extra context that you and your friends understand, but the normies don’t,” said Pearson.

Voicemod’s team has been encouraged by the increasing availability of voice-changing tech in games. Around a year ago, Arc Raiders launched its voice changer in beta but only offered ten voices at launch, and Voicemod offered their own tech to expand those options. 

“[Gamers] are social beings, they don’t want to have the default skin. They want to have their own skin customized,” Pearson said. “If the game just gives you 5-10 skins, you’re gonna want the next one, you want to differentiate yourself.”

The company’s Voicelab enables further voice tweaking with fun effects. One could, if they wanted, change their voice to sound like they were wearing a helmet in a cave inside a volcano — wacky but evocative sonic context placing the person in a specific space and circumstance. It enhances expression and storytelling and uses AI to do it. But not the AI you’re thinking of.

AI has been at the heart of Voicemod — but not generative AI

There’s no denying that technological advancement has enabled voice generation, but Voicemod came long before that. It was founded 14 years ago, using digital sound processing to alter voices, launching first on an iPhone 3GS, Bordanova explained. 

What their tech enabled that traditional DSP could not is changing the timbre of the voice — its tone, color and personality. Using math, Voicemod’s tech could change a vocal signal in ways that would simulate changing the human organs that naturally shape one’s voice, like elongating or shrinking the vocal cords or altering the width of your throat or nose. 

More traditional AI powered Voicemod’s older methods of voice changing, which improved thanks to technological developments. The company’s advantage was to be one of the first to invest heavily in AI’s use in voice changing, Bordanova said. 

“There was something unique, something very special, that would evolve us from being a voice changer to having fun with friends online, into giving real utility for a 24/7 use case,” Bordanova said. 

What he clarifies is that Voicemod’s tech isn’t based on generative AI, unlike the tech behind voice processing tricks like Google’s live translation. Instead, their language models are around 20 megabytes in weight, and take about a week to train. Unlike the immense large language models used in generative AI, Voicemod’s are small enough to fully download on phones and other client-side devices. They can be consulted immediately on device for 42 millisecond latency, rather than need to go to the cloud.

That doesn’t mean they’ll never use LLMs — but the use case they’re envisioning is as a glorified assistant helping people find the right toggles and settings to get the voice they want from existing choices. 

“You can type, I want the voice of SpongeBob and the LLM would pick the right effect and parameters and just create the voice for us,” Bordanova said. 

Voicemod

Expression on the go, through your phone to your digital life

Back in March at MWC 2026, I chatted with Bordanova and Pearson when they brought out a prototype for the Key Pocket, the follow-up to the company’s earlier Voicemod Key, a dongle device that aimed to help change voices for console play. Even in its cruder form, the Key Pocket felt special. 

As even the prototype was MagSafe compatible, I clipped it to the back of my own iPhone 15 Pro Max. Even if the device wasn’t far enough along to be usable with software, I could still simulate how it would feel in action with my phone rotated sideways, as if I had it active while gaming. The row of buttons rested below my fingers, easy to press if I wanted to tweak my voice or trigger vocal or sound effects. The volume wheel was nice and accessible. If I was streaming or chatting with my friends, the Key Pocket would be a nice accessory to have.

While a lot of gaming happens at home on PC and console, mobile gaming is a huge sector. The Key Pocket is a neat tool for gamers who either play on the go or who opt to play on phones for other reasons — possibly because they can’t afford pricey bigger platforms, which have only gotten more expensive since the RAM shortage. Odds are good that the phone in many gamers’ pockets can play the games they want, and the Key Pocket could help with their so-called sonic identity.

Voicemod’s goal goes beyond the Key Pocket to eventually integrate their tech at a system level, so that anyone booting up a computer or phone could use the tens of thousands of voices created by the Voicemod community (along with the filters and sound effects) to modify their aural appearance anywhere on the device. 

“The last frontier is to get rid of the hardware,” Bordanova said.

Expanding Voicemod’s tech across a device’s software and apps would broaden its appeal — imagine not just customizing your voice in games and voice chats with friends, but work Zooms and other calls. Having the same options and interface available everywhere you could use your voice would open up possibilities for folks who’ve never thought about tweaking their voices.

But any mobile gamer will tell you that external controls make a world of difference compared to on-screen digital buttons. Integrating voice tech into the back end of devices is good, but having the Key Pocket soundboard at the touch of your fingers is a far more tactile and responsive set of controls. For streamers and presenters on the go who rely on exact timing, the Key Pocket is a neat solution. Sometimes all you need is an attractively designed gadget to expose folks to new tech possibilities — and in this case, the potential to express themselves online in a way they may not have considered before.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Lumb
						

						

							Managing Editor, Mobile

Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. title: Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers
snippet: Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation. more…
fullText:
Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation.

Free trials are a pretty standard practice across the industry when it comes to subscriptions, and the general understanding is that you’re getting full access to the same subscription you are later set to pay for unless there’s an upfront stipulation about restrictions.

And that’s where things are getting a bit messy with Google’s AI Pro subscription.

Google One AI Pro is a $19.99/month subscription that delivers access to expanded Gemini usage limits, 5TB of storage across Google products, and bundles in other subscriptions such as Google Home Premium, Health Premium, and YouTube Premium Lite. Earlier this year, we called AI Pro “one of the best deals in tech today.”

	

But the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon to Google’s Antigravity development tool put a spotlight on a restriction on AI Pro’s free trials. Put simply, they’re limited compared to paid subscribers, and it’s not something Google made abundantly clear.

There are two specific downsides with a Google One AI Pro trial compared to an actively paid subscription. As mentioned, Antigravity on AI Pro trials leaves out Gemini 4 Argon. Google has a page that specifically puts a trial account in a completely different bucket compared to a paid AI Pro plan, and it treats the trial as a free user with expanded usage limits rather than a full user as @evowizz was one of the first to point out.

The other restriction is YouTube Premium Lite, which is not available for Google One AI Pro trial users until they start paying.

In Google’s defense, this is technically spelled out on support documents. The YouTube Premium Lite restriction, for example, is clearly spelled out as Google says that the “benefit is unavailable until trials of Google AI Pro conclude and you convert to a paid subscription.” But, as far as we can see, this is not disclosed as clearly at the time of sign-up or alongside advertising of the AI Pro trials.

Another loss here is the lack of Google One’s 10% cashback (store credit) perk in the Google Store, which is lacking in free trials. That one is certainly easier to see the reasoning behind, though.

The Google Store touts the Pixel 11’s AI Pro trial as delivering “expanded usage limits in Gemini, access to Gemini in Google apps, and 5 TB of cloud storage,” as well as Health Premium. Nowhere does Google promise the YouTube perks, but the wording around Gemini also lacks any hint at the restriction found in Antigravity. Pages including offer details also lack any mention of this.

As mentioned, Google hands out free, extended trials to AI Pro all over the place. Just a few active examples include:

6 months free with the purchase of a Pixel 11

12 months free with the purchase of a Googlebook

6 months free for select Verizon customers

12 months free with Chromebook Plus or 3 months with any other Chromebook

6 months free with the purchase of a Galaxy Z Fold 8

And that’s just a few examples – you can absolutely find more.

	

Google explicitly lists all of these trials at their full monthly value (i.e. $119 value for Pixel’s 6-month trial) despite the restricted access that trial users see.

While Google has not addressed the somewhat misleading nature of the AI Pro trial restrictions, one Googler responded to the other headache that exists here – you can’t just press a button to start paying for AI Pro if you’re on a trial. You either have to wait for the trial to end, or reach out to Google for help converting your account. 

What do you think of the situation?

title: YouTube’s contextual AI search rolls out to all users on Android and iOS in US
snippet: “Ask YouTube” is no longer a YouTube Premium feature as the conversational AI search becomes available on mobile Android and iOS devices. more…
fullText:
“Ask YouTube” is no longer a YouTube Premium feature as the conversational AI search becomes available on mobile Android and iOS devices.

Today, Google announced the Ask YouTube feature would be widely rolling out to mobile users, in addition to TV instances of the YouTube app. Unlike before, Ask YouTube will now be accessible to all users, not just Premium subscribers. 

Access to some form of contextual AI model has been available on YouTube for a while, dating back to 2023. Since then, Google has settled on an “Ask YouTube” button that lets users ask questions about videos to get more insight. The rollout has been limited, with TVs and Premium users getting access first.

The feature has evolved a bit, and it’s taken on a conversation-oriented presentation. It isn’t limited to questions about the video or what happens at which timestamp. It’s powered through Gemini, so its answers go beyond strictly what’s in the video you’re watching.

	

Google also notes that users will be able to use Ask YouTube from the watch page in their Shorts feed and during live streams, but that feature will be a later release. For the time being, users in the US can expect Ask YouTube to show up on your mobile Android or iOS device soon as it rolls out to more users. Google says it plans to gradually expand availability.

Americans have a privacy problem, which shouldn’t come as any surprise. Between Ring’s now scrapped interconnected doorbell feature “Search Party,” the unprecedented backlash around Flock cameras, and data brokers quietly selling away our identities, individual privacy is center stage for Americans right now. I would go as far as to make it the inaugural Security Bite ‘Theme of the Year.’

Yet despite all of that, a new survey from data removal service Incogni found that 45% of the 1,517 U.S. adults polled say they aren’t concerned about their online privacy. That wasn’t even the best part of this survey though…

Among people who said they have nothing to hide, 58% would refuse to hand a stranger their unlocked phone for any amount of money, 39% cover the camera on their phone or laptop, and nearly half wouldn’t hand over their text messages to the government or “Big Tech,” even for three months of their income.

I asked Ron Zayas, founder and CEO of Ironwall by Incogni, what’s actually going on here, and he basically replied that privacy only feels abstract until it isn’t.

“We take privacy for granted, until it means that someone will read our messages, charge us more, put us in danger or disclose intimate details about us,” he told me. “But the reality is, all of that is privacy.” He also thinks companies lean on that gap on purpose, pointing out that if a privacy policy actually said “download this app and we will go through your contacts, suck in your photos, analyze your habits and share those details with anyone willing to pay us,” most of us would pause. Instead, they open with “we value your privacy” and bury the rest in legalese.

The survey also found that 65% of respondents have no idea how many websites they’re registered on, and honestly, I’m not sure I could tell you mine either. We’ve all spent the last decade or so creating accounts for things we used once and forgot about, and every one of them is still holding onto something. You can’t protect data you don’t remember giving away, right?

So I asked Zayas where someone on an iPhone or Mac should start if they want to cut that down without going full underground, and his answer was more Apple-friendly than I was expecting. “Apple has some pretty good safety protocols, much better than Google in my opinion, and makes them far easier to access,” he said. “Turn off as much of ad personalization, location sharing and contact sharing as you can. It only takes a moment.” He also recommends treating your phone number like you would a credit card number. Allowing an app to have access to your contacts will also give it your own.

Zayas put it well when he said that believing you have to “go full bunker in Montana” to have any privacy is a fallacy companies push to make people feel helpless, and I agree with him. If you live in California, the CCPA and Delete Act let you force a good chunk of your data off the market for free. For everyone else, a few minutes to clean things up in Privacy & Security can go a long way. The survey honestly put it better by saying, most of us already act like our privacy matters, so we might as well stop saying it doesn’t.

title: Surprise! Meta and Apple Worked Together on a New Open-Source AI Model
snippet: Think of Muse Spark Open as the result of Meta and Apple’s enemies-to-lovers arc.
fullText:
It’s the enemies-to-lovers trope, tech edition. Two tech titans have teamed up to create a new open-weights AI model. Meta is the owner of the new AI model, called Muse Spark Open, and it worked with Apple’s hardware team to ensure the AI model can run efficiently on the M5 Mac Studio Ultra. 

Muse Spark Open is an open-weights AI model, which means developers can understand how it works and customize it to their needs. It has a robust 42 billion active parameters and a context window of a million tokens, with multimodal capabilities that Meta says are good at agentic and coding tasks. Translation: It’s a big model that can handle different kinds of tasks, including powering AI agents, aimed at engineers and developers. The model’s weights are publicly available now on Hugging Face under Meta’s Muse Model license.

Note that if you want to run the model on Apple computers, it requires two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips. Right now, the base price for a device with the M5 Ultra chip (with 96GB of memory and 1TB of storage) starts at $5,499 each. If you want the device to have the full 512GB of RAM — which isn’t even on sale yet — it’s going to be far more expensive. Safe to say, as 256GB of RAM adds $4,000 to the price, that it would be a pricey investment.

			

More from CNET

Meta and Apple could not have taken more divergent paths in the AI race, or even in the pre-AI era. Apple has been hesitant to throw itself into AI development, whereas Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg couldn’t push his company fast enough, burning through billions of dollars to do so. Apple’s decades-long focus on privacy, while not perfect, is existentially at odds with Meta’s entire targeted advertising business model reliant on collecting as much information on its users as possible. Remember when Apple offered iPhone owners the ability to opt out of app tracking and cost Meta $10 billion in 2022?

But this new collaboration is a clear sign that both companies are determined to travel down their set paths in the AI race: Meta, to build open-weights AI models, and Apple, to build the hardware needed to run AI. Or as Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, told Axios, “We’re excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again.” In X posts, Zuckerberg put it a bit more diplomatically; new Apple CEO John Ternus focused on the reason for the team-up, namely on-device AI.

Meta’s new open-weight model, Muse Spark Open, can run on Apple’s Mac Studio.Mark Zuckerberg

On-device AI is a way to run AI models and tools without relying on a cloud service. It requires a little more setup than simply opening up your ChatGPT app, but developers and businesses can configure the AI system to keep their data more secure. Depending on the scale of the operation and hardware used, it can also be a cheaper, long-term option than continually paying a monthly subscription.

It’s not totally surprising to see Apple taking part in AI development, despite its own meager AI tools. The Californian company has carved out a place in the AI race through its hardware. At the beginning of 2026, when tech circles were excitedly using the OpenClaw agent, Apple’s Mac Minis were the computer of choice for many AI fans. During Apple’s hardware launches, including the M5 MacBook Air in March, Apple boasted that its chip tech could power impressive performance, and CNET’s testing mostly verifies those promises. The Mac Studio, released in August, is the latest example of Apple focusing on hardware capable of running compute-intensive AI tasks.

title: Gemini AI Plus subscribers will lose access to Pro models next month
snippet: Google has begun emailing Gemini AI Plus members to inform them when their Gemini subscription will no longer include access to the advanced models – just Flash. more…
fullText:
Google has begun emailing Gemini AI Plus members to inform them when their Gemini subscription will no longer include access to the advanced models – just Flash.

A change in Gemini’s subscription model was announced earlier this month. It came right before Google’s new Argon model went live and became the new high-performance offer in Gemini. The company made it clear that Gemini 4 Argon would be included for AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers, but it also said AI Plus members would lose access to AI Pro entirely.

According to one user on Reddit, Google has begun emailing AI Plus subscribers to let them know Gemini Pro models would be excluded from the AI Plus tier starting on November 13. The email lists Flash-Lite and Flash as the only two options after that date.

We wanted to let you know about changes to the models that you can access with your Google AI Plus plan.

Starting on ﻿1﻿3﻿ ﻿N﻿o﻿v﻿e﻿m﻿b﻿e﻿r﻿ ﻿2﻿0﻿2﻿6﻿, the ability to select Pro models in both the Gemini app and AI Mode in Google Search will only be available to Google AI Pro subscribers and above. You’ll still have access to our latest Flash-Lite model and Flash, built for speed and intelligence. Your previous chats using the Pro model can be continued with a different model.

To learn more about these changes, you can visit our Help Centre article for additional details. You can manage or cancel your subscription at any time.

Thank you for being a Google AI Plus subscriber.

– The Google One team

A couple of others report getting the same email, which puts a pin on exactly when the Gemini AI Plus plan changes.

	

The $4.99/month option will give users access to just two models, while the $19.99/month tier gains access to Argon, leaving a bigger gap between the two. Google is still keeping the free plan around, which leaves everyone with access to Flash-lite.

Of course, these subscriptions tie into Google Workspace for cloud storage and other perks, like YouTube Premium. Still, the $4.99/month plan seemed like a good deal for those who wanted access to more capable models for more than just passive chats.

title: Amazon launches two Bee AI recorders to remember everything you say
snippet: Just over a year after acquiring the AI company, Bee, Amazon has officially unveiled two of its first AI wearables, so you never forget what was said. more…
fullText:
Just over a year after acquiring the AI company, Bee, Amazon has officially unveiled two of its first AI wearables, so you never forget what was said.

Amazon announced two models: the Bee Frontier and the Bee Eclipse. Both can be considered wearables, with one taking on a bracelet form factor that works just fine clipped to a shirt. The Eclipse is a magnetic version of the always-listening device for use with Qi2 or MagSafe-equipped phones.

The Frontier is not dissimilar to the first preview Bee introduced before it was purchased by Amazon. At the time, the company had seemingly high hopes for being a genuine cornerstone of people’s lives to make their lives easier.

Amazon says both models are designed with “privacy principles” in mind, noting that a visible LED indicates when the Bee Frontier or Eclipse is listening. That’s what they do, after all. Both are designed to stay active and compile your ideas, thoughts, and even nonsense into reminders or notes, based on what Bee’s AI model decides you might need.

	

All of that can be found in the companion app, whether on mobile or desktop. Users can connect their Google Account to let it access emails and calendar information. That feeds into the selling idea that Bee becomes your personal assistant so you don’t miss out on a thing.

As for hardware, the Bee Frontier wearable is IP67 and rated for seven days of battery. The magnetic Eclipse model is able to power through a longer workload with up to 21 days of battery on a charge.

Of course, Amazon also added Alexa+ and Amazon.com integration into how the Bee wearables operate. The devices will be able to surface products based on your anticipated needs. That’s fun.

The Bee Frontier is available now for $74.99, while the Bee Eclipse will goi on sale “soon” starting at $99.99.

title: Apple Intelligence reportedly coming to China in December, but without Siri AI
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple plans to finally launch Apple Intelligence in China in December, although some important features could still be missing. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple plans to finally launch Apple Intelligence in China in December, although some important features could still be missing. Here are the details.

Apple Intelligence to see limited launch in China with iOS 27.3

Earlier today, a report from the South China Morning Post claimed that Chinese regulators had approved the use of Alibaba’s AI models to power Apple Intelligence, following preliminary approval for the platform’s rollout in July.

The report noted that the timing of the approval was particularly relevant, as the iPhone Duo is scheduled to launch in China next week.

Now, Bloomberg reports that Apple “is planning to launch Apple Intelligence in the region in December as part of an upcoming iOS 27.3 update,” although the launch “will exclude the new Siri AI assistant and other features announced this year,” according to the publication’s sources.

The move comes after a lengthy and complicated effort to bring Apple Intelligence to China, where local regulations governing AI-generated content, security assessments, and algorithm registration have forced Apple to take a different approach than in other markets.

Here’s Bloomberg:

In order to get Apple Intelligence approved, the company had to make some concessions. Unlike in other countries, the platform has guardrails developed with China’s Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., including a filter that allows the government to approve ongoing updates to the AI models. Apple is also working with Baidu Inc. on features related to search and Siri.

On Sept. 29, Apple received Chinese permits allowing recent iPhones to support the use of Apple Intelligence and Alibaba AI models, including Tongyi Wanxiang and Qwen.

The report notes that Apple Intelligence’s launch in China will not feature “the company’s in-house image-generation tools,” while certain “features for generating text will also be limited in some applications.”

According to Bloomberg, the initial rollout will include Genmoji for creating custom emoji, Apple’s AI-powered notification summaries, writing tools, and the Clean Up feature in Photos, which lets users remove unwanted objects from images.

The report notes that it is unclear whether these features will be enough to win over Chinese consumers, as local smartphone makers have already introduced their own AI capabilities:

With AI services proliferating on rival phones from Huawei Technologies Co., Xiaomi Corp., Oppo Guangdong Mobile Telecommunications Corp., Vivo Mobile Communication Co. and others in China, it’s unclear how much Apple will benefit from launching a two-year-old set of relatively basic AI features in the country.

Interestingly, today’s report came just one day after Apple said in the footnotes of its HomeView announcement that it is “working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward” to launch Siri AI in Europe, where the assistant also remains unavailable due to regulatory issues.

title: Gemini app rolling out Gemini 4 Argon to AI Pro and AI Ultra
snippet: Following the announcement at the end of September, Gemini 4 Argon is starting to roll out to the Gemini app, Google Antigravity, and more. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement at the end of September, Gemini 4 Argon is starting to roll out to the Gemini app, Google Antigravity, and more.

Gemini app 

In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Argon is available for both Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Last month, initial availability was just for the Ultra ($99.99+) tier. 

Google says to expect “frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows” in the app. Additionally:

“Argon answers questions more directly with less hedging, doesn’t repeat itself more than necessary, and skips clichés throughout the responses.” Additionally, it “follows style instructions more reliably than any of our previous Gemini models.”

“For longer tasks, it keeps you in the loop by sharing its progress more often and more effectively.”

Given the “major improvements” in coding performance, Google is letting users “switch between chatting and coding” within the Gemini app for macOS. Users will specifically have direct access to Antigravity’s agentic coding interface in the consumer client for building apps, web experiences, and more.

	

Meanwhile, there will be a new toggle in the main chat window that lets you switch from chat to tasks (previously Spark). As of today, AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers will see 3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.8 Flash, 3.1 Pro, and 4 Argon in the model picker.

AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers can also access Gemini 4 Argon in AI Mode.

Google Antigravity + more

	

In the Antigravity desktop app and Antigravity CLI, the new model requires AI Ultra. Google today shared more examples of how it has been using Argon with its internal version of Antigravity across Chrome, Gemma, YouTube, and more:

“Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase. Piping multiple clean code changes at a time, Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome’s billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes.”

“Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the upstream pull requests (optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes.”

“Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms.”

AI Ultra is also required for Argon access in AI Studio and Android Studio (Canary).

Argon is available in the Gemini API at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30, 2026. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

On the science front, Google is offering 10,000 scientists the “highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free of charge for 6 months.” Applications are now open.

title: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
snippet: Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won't play nice? In recent weeks, users of services like Meta's Muse, xAI's Grok, OpenAI's Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking ticket … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice?

In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak, suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.

Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup, raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.”

Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August. Amazon has since filed an amended complaint.

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems

This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon, which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok, Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are.

“Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge. “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.”

Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.

The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment.

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.”

The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.

While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”

title: Meta says it has fixed an issue that let its Ray-Ban smart glasses record on their own
snippet: As privacy complaints continue to dominate the conversation around Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, the company is now fixing an issue that was letting the glasses record on their own without the user prompting the recording. more…
fullText:
As privacy complaints continue to dominate the conversation around Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, the company is now fixing an issue that was letting the glasses record on their own without the user prompting the recording.

A number of Ray-Ban Meta users on Reddit note that, recently, their glasses have been invoking Meta AI and, in turn, voice recording, without prompts. The “Hey Meta” wake word was not used and, for some, not even enabled. One user says this happened across three separate pairs of glasses. 

The glasses still alert users to the recordings by lighting up the LED on the inner frame of the glasses, but it’s obviously a bit concerning to randomly have the glasses start recording on their own, even if it is audio only. 

Speaking to Android Authority, Meta confirmed that the issue has been “resolved.”

	

This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.

The cause isn’t mentioned, but it comes at a time where Meta’s smart glasses are under continual scrutiny for privacy. Meta, in trying to correct its course, has made adjustments to its glasses including rolling out a mandatory update that disables the camera on its glasses if someone tampers with the LED privacy light.

fullText:
A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra split in a slightly different direction. Instead of a display panel treatment with an anti-gflare coating, Samsung decided to pack an entirely different feature into the panel itself.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display allows users to block certain aspects of the screen from nearby onlookers, effectively circumventing the privacy screen protector so many users opt for.

According to Time‘s “best inventions of 2026” collection, the Galaxy S26 Ultra gets its plaudits for not the phone’s performance necessarily, but the Privacy Display. The listing quotes Samsung’s SVP of Mobile Product Management, who points to its flexible nature.

	

It’s undoubtedly a cool piece of display tech. The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display not only blocks side-angle viewing, but it can do so in isolated portions of the screen to block PIN codes or notifications that drop from the top shade in Android.

It has some drawbacks, though, as we’ve pointed out before. It can be a little inconsistent in certain lighting conditions, and sometimes screen elements can look off. But it’s cool, and a nice addition to a phone that sits at a price range we now consider more affordable than what we’re probably getting here soon.

Time‘s piece goes on to list a couple of other familiar devices, like a lengthy segment on the iPhone Duo, propping it up rather highly. Another product we’re happy to see is the Clicks Power Keyboard.

AS for whether the Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra will get a Privacy Display, rumors suggest it could happen. Time will tell as Samsung plans to launch the devices early next year.

title: Supreme Court Weighs Major Video Privacy Case
snippet: A 1988 federal law could bar tech companies from using video viewing data for targeted ads without explicit user consent.
fullText:
It’s usually legal for an American company to gather your personal data and use it to target you with an advertisement, and many online companies rely on this to make money. But a data privacy case now before the US Supreme Court may upend the longstanding practice of personal data collection for use in targeted ads.

The case, Salazar v. Paramount Global, stems from a 2022 class action lawsuit filed by Michael Salazar. At issue is a free digital newsletter Salazar signed up for, which was published by 247Sports.com, a college sports news website owned by Paramount Global. 

The website included a tracker that shared Salazar’s video viewing history with Facebook without his consent. Salazar says that Paramount did this illegally. But the federal law that Salazar says Paramount violated is a 1988 Reagan-era act governing videotape rentals. 

			

More from CNET

Home video leak

In 1987, President Ronald Reagan nominated Robert Bork for a seat on the Supreme Court, though the nomination was famously rejected by the Senate. During Bork’s confirmation hearings, a writer for the alt-weekly Washington City Paper convinced the manager at a video rental store to slip him Bork’s video-rental history, which the paper published along with commentary on Bork’s film choices. 

While Bork’s rental history was fairly boring, the story and its fallout eventually led Congress to pass the Video Privacy Protection Act.  The law was created for analog media, but Salazar’s team argues that it also applies to digital media, such as website content. Essentially, if it’s illegal for a video rental store to share your customer information, why are tech companies allowed to do it?

“The Supreme Court’s decision in Salazar v. Paramount Global will affect the privacy rights of millions of people across the country,” Salazar’s lawyer, Joshua I. Hammack, told CNET via email. “Ordinary consumers might be shocked to learn how much of their online activity is tracked, disclosed, and sold. As I argued to the Supreme Court, the Video Protection Privacy Act was designed to give Americans control over our private information, even as companies like Paramount seek new ways to monetize it.”

Defining a consumer

Paramount’s argument centers on how a “consumer” is defined in the Video Privacy Protection Act, with the company asserting that the definition doesn’t include people who subscribed to a free digital newsletter. This was the reason the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the lawsuit. 

“The Sixth Circuit correctly rejected that effort,” a case document filed by Paramount reads. “The court of appeals dismissed Salazar’s complaint against 247Sports on the grounds that Salazar is not a ‘consumer’ because he did not ‘rent, purchase, or subscribe’ to the delivery of any ‘video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.’”

The National Retail Federation, Retail Litigation Center, Motion Picture Association, Entertainment Software Association, Meta and the US Chamber of Commerce have all written the court in support of Paramount’s position. 

A representative for Paramount Global didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Why do I care who has my data?

Neil Richards, Koch Distinguished Professor and director of the Cordell Institute at the University of Washington School of Law, believes the Video Protection Privacy Act applies to this case and should be enforced. 

“Regulating surveillance-based ads, whether by banning them, by giving people meaningful choice to opt out entirely, or through interpretations of existing laws like the VPPA, would be the single best thing we could do for the privacy protections of the average internet user,” Richards told CNET via email.

Although the act was enacted back when Blockbuster Video stores blanketed the country, Richards said the law was intended for future use.

“Congress intentionally drafted the law in a far-sighted way to protect the activity of private video-watching, regardless of the technologies or formats used to watch,” Richards said. “A win for Salazar would be a much-needed win for internet privacy and a much-needed pushback to the greed of surveillance tech companies.”

What could change with data tracking

Even if Salazar wins, any restrictions on tracking could be limited, as the case is specifically about whether it’s illegal to share someone’s digital video-watching history. 

“I think that video content probably isn’t actually influencing that many ads.” Justin Brookman, the director of technology policy for Consumer Reports, told CNET over the phone. “Most targeted ads are like retargeted ads based on, ‘you looked at this product, and therefore the product’s going to follow you around.’”

Applying the act here probably won’t sink online targeted ads, Brookman says, even if the law is interpreted fairly broadly. But Brookman says he hopes the case culminates in new privacy protections for internet users, as long as those new protections don’t place the burden on internet users. 

“I think just a prohibition on sharing [personal data] would be a better result than forcing people through a million consent screens in every site they go to,” Brookman said. 

A chilling effect

Tracking and sharing the histories of the videos people watch could negatively affect internet users’ behavior, according to Eric Null, director of the privacy and data project at the Center for Democracy and Technology.

“Watching videos is an expressive activity, and having those videos tracked, shared, and sold to third parties for various and potentially nefarious purposes will chill that expression,” Null said in an email to CNET. 

“The VPPA does cover free online pre-recorded videos, but the statute nonetheless has significant limitations in its scope that can only be rectified by updating our privacy laws,” he said. “We could, of course, do so through a comprehensive privacy law that includes protections for video viewing.”

A Supreme Court ruling is expected in 2027.

But a data privacy case now before the US Supreme Court may upend the longstanding practice of personal data collection for use in targeted ads.

The case, Salazar v. Paramount Global, stems from a 2022 class action lawsuit filed by Michael Salazar. At issue is a free digital newsletter Salazar signed up for, which was published by 247Sports.com, a college sports news website owned by Paramount Global.

title: YouTube Music rolling out AI labels in the Now Playing screen
snippet: In response to more AI-generated content appearing on streaming services, YouTube Music is adding a new AI label directly to the player. more…
fullText:
In response to more AI-generated content appearing on streaming services, YouTube Music is adding a new AI label directly to the player.

When a song is “created primarily using generative AI,” you’ll soon see a label on the Now Playing screen. This includes “using a generative model to create the composition and vocals.” The goal is to “make it as easy as possible for viewers and listeners to have the right information and clarity when it comes to the music they listen to.”

It appears just below the song name next to the artist/channel. This “AI” badge with an info icon opens a “How this was made” bottom sheet. 

YouTube Music explains how this was “Made with AI: This audio was altered or fully generated using AI” with a link to learn more. 

	

YouTube is using its own detection tools and “teaming up with music partners” to identify AI-generated tracks. 

The rollout starts today. In the future, these AI labels for music will come to the main YouTube app.

title: Gemini 4 Argon is now rolling out to Google’s Antigravity for AI Pro subscribers
snippet: Google is now rolling out support for Gemini 4 Argon to Antigravity, its AI coding tool. more…
fullText:
Google is now rolling out support for Gemini 4 Argon to Antigravity, its AI coding tool.

Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s latest flagship AI model, announced at the end of September and having widely rolled out to users earlier this week. Now, it’s also available within Antigravity.

Antigravity is an agentic development platform, as Google describes it, which leverages AI and agents to assist in coding and building apps. Google announced that Argon would be available in Antigravity earlier this week, and it’s now actively rolling out to AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers – we’re seeing it live on our end, too.

Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers

In a post on Twitter/X, Google adds that there’s “a separate weekly-only Argon quota” on top of the existing quota for Gemini 3.8 Flash, meaning you’ll be able to use the model that best suits your needs. Google says that Argon is “designed to tackle your hardest problems.”

	

Google also provided a host of examples of how Argon in Antigravity has been used internally, including:

YouTube comment optimization: Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms.

Debugging Wing drone physics simulator: Argon in Antigravity reviewed Wing’s proprietary internal drone physics simulator, reasoning through the underlying physics and math rather than just the structure of the code. It highlighted areas for improved physics simulations and proposed 18 targeted modelling improvements across aerodynamics, propulsion, and structural dynamics to resolve long-standing legacy issues.

Burning down the backlog: Argon in Antigravity took an aging queue of 134 open bug reports spanning multiple services, and ran agents to work out which were still real, cross-referencing commit histories, checking whether candidate fixes actually reached production, and inspecting live telemetry for whether the error still occurs. In under 3 hours it closed 97 stale or duplicate bugs with documented commit proof (a 72.4% queue reduction) and sorted the remaining 37 by owner with no unassigned tickets left.

Migrating legacy code: For decades, vital scientific research has been locked inside fragile legacy codebases like Fortran. Using a custom skill within Antigravity, a team deployed Argon to map and execute a complete rewrite into modern Rust. Argon autonomously delivered the modernized codebase, achieving a 1.8x performance boost and memory safety while giving scientists a robust foundation for future work.

Performing security audits: Argon in Antigravity was used to audit a batch of access-control changes. Argon traced how permissions actually flowed at runtime rather than just reading the code diff, and found four critical security bugs. Two earlier frontier models had audited the identical code and both concluded there were zero security holes.

Triaging production support tickets: Argon in Antigravity batch-processes dozens of tickets from an on-call rotation. It sorts them by issue type, tracing root causes through the code and logs, proposing fixes and drafting the replies for human approval. This has freed up 2-3 hours per shift, enabling the team to focus on resolving issues faster.

Marketing website localization: The Antigravity DevRel team used Argon in Antigravity to localize hundreds of pages of developer documentation into 17 languages in a matter of hours. This improved the accessibility and UX of the website by shrinking a multi-week process down to hours and shifting human effort exclusively to high-quality review.

Accelerating data center pipeline modernization: Demonstrating how AI-augmented execution helps teams do more with less, a Data Science Technical Program Manager leveraged Argon in Antigravity to fast-track development of a 3,200-line Google Data Center fleet analytics pipeline (Python, SQL, and dashboards) into production in days. Pairing with Argon to rapidly resolve complex multi-system edge cases, eliminate hardcoded legacy assets, and optimize timeseries queries against timeouts drove end-to-end efficiency — delivering a clean, production-grade, and extensible architecture for fleet-scale analytics.

Vetting sales prospects: Argon in Antigravity built an automated qualification workflow for an account executive in Ads sales that checks prospective company website traffic, confirms the site has clear conversion funnels, and cross-references the sales database to see whether the account is a qualified prospect. This reduced research time by 90%, saving the account executive upwards of 10 hours of manual work each week so they can spend time on direct client outreach instead.

Financial planning and analysis: With custom finance plugins, a finance lead used Argon in Antigravity for end-to-end financial reconciliations, budget tracking, contract extraction, and daily executive briefings across 80 separate workflows. Over seven business days, 15.5 hours of human direction produced about 335 human-equivalent hours of validated financial output, saving more than eight weeks of manual work.

title: Apple website suggested Siri AI may be coming to full size HomePods
snippet: The headline feature of the new HomePod mini 2 is support for Siri AI, something that won’t be available for the first-gen model. But there’s hope that existing full size HomePods may also get access to the smarter intelligent assistant. A leaker noticed two clues on Apple’s website seemingly pointing to this, but it’s possible that it was an error on the part of the company … more…
fullText:
The headline feature of the new HomePod mini 2 is support for Siri AI, something that won’t be available for the first-gen model. But there’s hope that existing full size HomePods may also get access to the smarter intelligent assistant.

A leaker noticed two clues on Apple’s website seemingly pointing to this, but it’s possible that it was an error on the part of the company … 

HomePod mini 2 with Siri AI

The HomePod mini 2 has the same design as its predecessor, other than refreshed colors. Internally, the S5 chip is replaced with an S10 one, and that provides access to Siri AI.

Not all of the processing is done on the device itself. Apple notes that full Siri AI support is dependent on pairing with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, HomePod mini can tap into a user’s personal context to help them find what they need in the moment.

Full-size HomePods may also get Siri AI

Leaker pdfu spotted a couple of indications on Apple’s website that support is also coming to existing full size HomePods – though likely only to 2nd-gen models.

First, there were the images used, where the color glow appeared to match that of the HomePod mini 2.

Big updates to the HomePod 2 product page this morning. May suggest support for Siri AI is coming.

The Siri examples now use Siri AI’s gradient style, and the refreshed glow matches Siri’s look on HomePod mini 2. pic.twitter.com/5X1sbwsC4T

— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 13, 2026

Second, alt text for one of the images described it as showing the “multi-colored Siri Al glow on top.”

9to5Mac’s Take

From a commercial perspective, Apple does like to hold back some software features from older devices in order to encourage upgrades. At the same time, the company is making a big push on Siri AI, likely to boost Services revenue once usage limits kick in on lower iCloud tiers.

It’s notable that Apple has replaced the images concerned, but this doesn’t provide much clue as to whether it was an error or simply an announcement the company isn’t yet ready to make. Even on the new HomePod mini 2 speakers, the Siri AI update will follow at a later date. It’s possible that support for their bigger brother could be announced at the same time.

The optimistic view would be that Apple isn’t requiring Apple TV owners to upgrade in order to get access to Siri AI, which might provide a clue to the company’s thinking. The update is coming to second-generation devices and up, and that may well point to the same story with the full-size HomePod 2.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Nothing reportedly launching two pairs of smart glasses, one with barely any AI
snippet: A reliable source says that Nothing is building out its own AI smart glasses that feature ChatGPT integration, a camera, and two very different models. more…
fullText:
A reliable source says that Nothing is building out its own AI smart glasses that feature ChatGPT integration, a camera, and two very different models.

WinFuture’s Roland Quandt says on Bluesky that Nothing is preparing to launch two new smart glasses models, and they sound wildly different.

One pair would be similar to the Ray-Ban Meta lineup with a built-in camera and AI features such as translation. While Nothing as an avid Android user might seem like one to hop on the Android XR train, it sounds like that’s probably not the case given Quandt says these are bringing integration with ChatGPT rather than Gemini. That’s not a new pivot on Nothing’s part, though, as the company has been building out ChatGPT integration for a while in its other products.

The other pair of smart glasses, though, would take a much simpler approach.

	

These would work as a pair of headphones with the ability to take calls and interact with your phone’s voice assistant, but they’d lack a camera or any direct AI integrations. Both models are said to offer photochromic lenses, otherwise known as “transition” lenses and commonly found on other smart glasses.

Prior reporting on Nothing’s efforts to build smart glasses pinned a release date sometime in 2027. The dual strategy here is certainly interesting, especially given a recent report that suggested Nothing would go all-in on AI devices going forward.

title: I Test Home Security Tech. Here Are 4 Devices I Rely on to Guard My Porch
snippet: Porch security is the best, easiest safety project for anyone new to smart homes.
fullText:
Your front door is your first line of defense against, well, anything you don’t want in your home. It’s also one of the first places burglars check when they’re looking for an easy break-in, and the spot porch pirates watch if they think lucrative packages are going to show up. That means your door is also the best place to start improving home security, especially as the holidays ramp up and you get more visitors and deliveries.

Here’s the technology I use to protect my front door and porch, in four easy steps anyone can start with. You don’t need to install a full security system or pay a high monthly subscription for home monitoring with these devices, either. Setup is totally DIY and takes very little time, too. See which you should start with.

A smart lock to control access from anywhere

Smart locks add a new dimension to your security.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Old deadbolts do well, but any entryway can get a powerful upgrade by adding digital features via a smart lock. Smart locks allow you to control your front door lock from anywhere using your phone, as well as creating temporary passes for guests. They can support digital wallet keys for touchless unlocking, and many have keypads or fingerprint readers. Plus, you can enable settings like auto-locking, so you never have to worry about forgetting to lock the door.

			

More from CNET

Smart locks come in two flavors: retrofits that leave your deadbolt largely intact and only replace your indoor thumb turn, and full deadbolt replacements that give you new locking power, inside and out. Don’t worry about installation: If you’ve never installed a deadbolt before, the process is generally easy and doesn’t take much time. I have a full guide where you can find more details.

What models do you recommend?

Yale’s latest Assure lock ($260)

August’s easy retrofit ($109)

Schlage’s ultimate upgrade ($395)

A video doorbell for smart alerts about what’s happening

Tapo’s large doorbell offers unique visual options. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Say goodbye to dusty doorbells of the past. Today’s high-tech doorbells do far more than chime: Video doorbells keep an eye on your front porch, while also giving you a two-way audio intercom right on your phone to hold a conversation — or even let an LLM do the talking for you.

Video doorbells also have particularly useful object recognition features, sometimes even for free. That includes recognizing packages and alerting you whenever one shows up at your door, or when one suddenly vanishes. Video storage options can save recordings of key events, so you can check who came to the door if you need to.

These advanced doorbells come in both wired and wireless versions. I’m a fan of the battery-powered, wireless models, which you can set and angle to get just the right look at your porch, doormat and other key places. Many can also work with your current door chime, although you probably don’t need it anymore with phone-based chimes.

What models do you recommend?

Google Nest’s compact, universal battery model ($180)

Tapo’s 4K beast with local video storage ($220)

Blink’s ultra-affordable doorbell ($80)

A delivery box to protect packages

Yale’s delivery boxes are larger, so you need room for them in the right spots.

Tyler Lacoma

Package theft concerns have reignited a centuries-old tradition of protecting mail. Today’s modern delivery boxes are specifically designed to allow delivery people to put packages inside, but make it difficult or impossible for thieves to take packages out, through clever lock models, auto-locking, smart controls and other various tricks.

I’ve been using a delivery box myself for a couple of years and find it very handy, as long as you have the space by your door. Some versions even come weighted or screwed down if you’re worried about a porch pirate absconding with the entire box. It’s a good idea to put notes in your deliveries to use the box, since despite signs not all delivery people will notice it’s there.

As a final plus, these boxes also keep your packages protected from the elements, which is nice when you live in an area that gets frequent winter snowstorms, as I do. 

What models do you recommend?

Yale’s sturdy smart box ($335)

Hyve’s sleek pod ($297)

A smart bulb for powerful lighting

Smart bulbs are cheap, support multiple voice assistants and have lots of fun tricks.

Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Where front doors exist, there’s usually a light nearby, like an overhead porch light or a wall-mounted lamp, to illuminate the entryway and surrounding area. These lights can also get a major makeover if you switch to an LED smart bulb, which are available as both BR30 floodlights and standard A19 home bulbs.

These lights also give you phone app controls, which is more important than it might seem. With my apps, I can control brightness, set schedules for bulbs to turn on or off, and even adjust the color to whatever I want, say for a holiday event. All it takes is screwing in the bulb and connecting it to Wi-Fi, so you can be done in seconds.

If you feel like experimenting, you can usually link smart bulbs to other devices, too. For example, you could set the light to turn on automatically when a smart lock is unlocked, or when a security system is disarmed.

What models do you recommend?

GE Cync’s four-quadrant Dynamic Effect floodlight bulb ($21)

Wiz’s highly affordable standard-sized bulb 2-pack ($22)

Ecosmart’s durable, extra-large floodlight bulb 2-pack ($14)

Now that your front porch is up to date, take a look at the latest home AI tricks I’ve found are actually worth using and how to get them.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: Googlebook will improve support for Linux apps eventually, but it’s all about AI for now
snippet: Googlebook was always going to run into problems with app availability, but few expected the platform to regress its support for Linux apps from Chromebook’s fairly robust solution. In a blog post, Google reiterates that the “Linux Terminal Preview” on Googlebook isn’t for using Linux apps, but for building with AI. more…
fullText:
Googlebook was always going to run into problems with app availability, but few expected the platform to regress its support for Linux apps from Chromebook’s fairly robust solution. In a blog post, Google reiterates that the “Linux Terminal Preview” on Googlebook isn’t for using Linux apps, but for building with AI.

ChromeOS introduced support for Linux apps a few years ago, allowing users to install apps designed for Linux on their machines to expand what the laptops could do. Googlebook does not have this same support, with the Linux Terminal accessible and apps technically installable, but those apps now show up alongside Android and web apps, nor do they feature the same level of user-facing functionality.

In a blog post this week, Google reiterates that the priority around Linux support on Googlebook is, for now, focused on AI-aided app development. 

Today, getting the most out of AI workflows requires access to a terminal with a command line, even if someone doesn’t identify as a programmer or software developer. With Googlebook, we’re excited to help users express themselves and gain access to these tools. Googlebooks come with pre-installed tooling to get you going.

Google says that the Terminal is designed to be the “entry point” for AI agents so that tools like Google’s own Antigravity can use command-line tools within the Linux virtual machine. That setup also ensures your private files are isolated from the agent’s access (unless you grant access). 

	
	

The Linux Terminal implementation on Googlebook is “optimized for rapid prototyping, web development, scripting, and agentic workflows via CLI,” Google says, with a future focus on “building not only on Googlebook but also for your other devices” while also fine-tuning the experience for “heavier workloads.” 

Also directly mentioned is that Google is working on support for showing Linux GUI apps in the app launcher, which is the main downside to the current implementation. 

We can’t wait for the terminal and Linux VM to continue getting more capable over time, including Linux GUI app support with integration directly into the app launcher.

There’s no word on when this might arrive, but the focus right now is very much on AI and development. The rest of Google’s roadmap includes:

We are working hard to get you building not only on Googlebook but also for your other devices. In addition to the existing network passthrough and wireless ADB, USB passthrough and support for ADB over USB are coming, enabling local device debugging and more from our Linux VM and Antigravity. Learn more about Antigravity on Googlebook.

Our testers have been eager to run more complex tasks. To make this more seamless, we are adding dynamic memory and storage scaling for the VM.

We will be adding GPU/NPU hardware acceleration for heavier local workloads, allowing users to leverage the performance and power efficiency of dedicated hardware.

VM persistence and separation from the terminal window will better support long-running processes, when you want to take on more demanding agentic workloads.
