title: Google Fitbit Edge hands-on: Pixel Watch Lite, take two
snippet: Google’s new Fitbit Edge tracker launches later this month and, as we get our review together, here’s a quick hands-on look at the new middle child of Google’s wearable lineup. more…
fullText:
Google’s new Fitbit Edge tracker launches later this month and, as we get our review together, here’s a quick hands-on look at the new middle child of Google’s wearable lineup.

The Fitbit Edge sits in between the screen-less Fitbit Air and the pricey & premium Pixel Watch 5. It’s the same slot that Google last addressed with the Fitbit Charge 6 back in 2023, but it does bring some changes this time around that make it even more of a “Pixel Watch Lite” than the Charge 6 already was.

As detailed in our launch coverage, the Fitbit Edge’s biggest upgrade over prior Fitbit trackers is the screen.

Google announces $179 Fitbit Edge tracker with display, GPS

It’s a much bigger canvas that fits a lot more on it, including new software tweaks that make it feel a lot more like a Pixel Watch than the Charge did. That includes both the faces and the different panels that Google has already shown. I’m thrilled to see a tactile power button on the side, too, as that was one of my biggest frustrations on the last Charge (even though Abner actually preferred it).

	

The hardware as a whole is simple, and we’ll get to how it feels to wear at a later date – we’re not allowed to share any in-depth insights or impressions from use on the Edge just yet, so this is really just a hands-on look.

Fitbit Edge is a fitness tracker first, supporting the usual heart rate, sleep, and workout tracking, as well as featuring the same live connection to both the Google Health app and third-party equipment for heart rate broadcasting and workout tracking. But it does more than that. With its display, it can also display notifications and calls from your phone, and it also has GPS that works with Google Maps.

I’m a bit disheartened to see that Google Wallet isn’t supported as it was on the Fitbit Charge 6, so that’s certainly a knock for the Fitbit Edge in my book. As for how that affects the overall experience, we’ll have to actually get into use to see more.

	

Continuing the Pixel Watch trend, Fitbit Edge uses the same style of Active Band, though with a connector that’s ripped from the Charge series. I was also pleasantly surprised to see that the Edge uses the exact same charger as the Air – I’m not sure who would use these two side-by-side, but it might be nice if you have a companion using the other tracker.

We’ll be digging into the Fitbit Edge over the coming weeks, so stay tuned!

Fitbit Edge officially launches on October 27, so you can probably take a guess when you’ll see our review. Pre-orders are open now.

title: PSA: Apple’s official silicone iPhone Duo case will require adhesive to stick
snippet: iPhone Duo is just about a week away from launching, and now that preorders have opened, Apple’s official iPhone Duo accessories have started to hit stores for early purchases. After purchasing, some users have noticed that the silicone case has a little bit of a caveat. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is just about a week away from launching, and now that preorders have opened, Apple’s official iPhone Duo accessories have started to hit stores for early purchases. After purchasing, some users have noticed that the silicone case has a little bit of a caveat.

Apple designed two cases for iPhone Duo: a $79 silicone case, and a $129 folio case. This concern is about the former.

With the silicone case for iPhone Duo, you’ll actually need to expose adhesive on the case for it to stick to your iPhone. Apple decided to opt for adhesives rather than using magnets. Presumably, the case would fall off if you don’t use the adhesive. This isn’t a new concept for foldable cases.

The unfortunate thing about this is that you likely can’t swap cases or go caseless as easily, and even if you do, the adhesive wouldn’t be as effective after you take it off.

	

This isn’t a super major deal, but something to keep in mind if you’re going to purchase Apple’s official silicone case for iPhone Duo. On the other hand, Apple’s folio with kickstand does seem to be rather nice, though it does carry a premium price tag.

title: Pocket Casts app now available on Android TV
snippet: After first coming to Apple TV, the official Pocket Casts app is now available to download on Android TV and Google TV devices. more…
fullText:
After first coming to Apple TV, the official Pocket Casts app is now available to download on Android TV and Google TV devices.

Officially teased when launching for Apple TV, it has taken a few months to be converted for Android set-top boxes. Unlike casting from your phone or tablet, this is a native app built from the ground up to work once paired with an existing account.

The dedicated experience is tailored to your TV, with a few refinements, including a dedicated “Made for TV” section for video podcasts with promoted content and highlighted content that you can watch and listen to simultaneously. It looks almost identical to the Apple TV version from what we can glean.

You pair using a QR code, and all of your podcast subscriptions, playlists, and account data will be synced with the application. You’re able to start a podcast playing and then close the application or minimize it, and it will continue playing. Any upcoming podcasts in your queue will appear as quick links, allowing you to switch quickly or pick up where you left off, as playback information across your devices is retained.

	

It’s worth noting that this has taken a couple of weeks to become widely available, as the app was noted in a recent changelog. You may have difficulty when searching directly on a Google TV or Android TV device, but you can “force” Pocket Casts to download from a browser by selecting any of your connected devices on the Play Store.

title: WhatsApp takes on Zoom and Google Meet with guest calling
snippet: WhatsApp users can now invite others to join group and one-on-one calls even if they don’t have an account. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
WhatsApp users can now invite others to join group and one-on-one calls even if they don’t have an account. Here are the details.

’Free, end-to-end encrypted calls for everyone with no time limits’

Today, WhatsApp announced the official rollout of guest calling, a feature that lets users “invite anyone to join a WhatsApp call – even if they don’t have a WhatsApp account.”

According to WhatsApp, guests must always be approved by the call host before joining, whether it’s a one-on-one call or a group call with up to 32 participants.

Guests enter a waiting room before being admitted, and hosts can remove them at any time. Guests also cannot see other participants’ phone numbers, send messages, or invite additional people.

WhatsApp says guest calling supports features such as screen sharing, hand-raising, and emoji-based reactions. Guests can also join directly from a computer browser, without installing the app.

Here’s WhatsApp on the new feature:

To get started, navigate to the Calls tab in WhatsApp, select the “+” icon, create a call link, and send it to the people you want to talk to – colleagues, classmates, or tutor – without having to worry about what apps they have.

Today’s launch comes after WhatsApp expanded testing of a similar feature for text conversations earlier this year, allowing users to exchange end-to-end encrypted messages with people who don’t have a WhatsApp account. At the time, however, the feature didn’t support voice or video calls.

Back to today’s news, WhatsApp also announced it is working on integrations with Google Calendar and Outlook, which will allow users to create WhatsApp call links directly from their calendars and add them to event invitations. The feature will require a WhatsApp plugin and is expected to launch later this year.

by  Terrence O'Brien

Oct 17, 2026, 4:39 PM UTC

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

In 2024, Elon Musk promised to give away $1 million a day to a randomly selected registered voter in a swing state. That prompted legal challenges, raised questions about its legality, and drew lawsuits from two Arizona residents claiming the lottery was a fraud. Musk has now agreed to settle the two lawsuits filed in Austin, Texas, though the details of the settlement have not been made public.

The plaintiffs claim that when Musk announced the sweepstakes, he falsely claimed the prizes would be awarded randomly. Philadelphia’s District Attorney sued to stop the giveaway, claiming that Musk was running an illegal lottery. During a hearing, Chris Gober, a representative for Musk’s America PAC, told the judge that “The $1 million recipients are not chosen by chance … We know exactly who will be announced as the $1 million recipient today and tomorrow.”

That directly contradicted Musk’s claim that the drawings were random. The plaintiffs say they never would have signed the petition required to enter the giveaway if they had known it wasn’t random. They accused Musk and America PAC of using it as a ploy to obtain user data and said the petition “places no limitations on America PAC’s use of or sale of the personal data it collects, nor does it provide any additional information about the planned use of data.”

title: Apple’s two HomeViews have one big hidden difference
snippet: Today Apple unveiled HomeView, its long-awaited smart home hub. The HomeView comes in two distinct models, one with a domed speaker base and the other designed for wall mounting. But there’s a hidden feature difference beyond the form factors. more…
fullText:
Today Apple unveiled HomeView, its long-awaited smart home hub. The HomeView comes in two distinct models, one with a domed speaker base and the other designed for wall mounting. But there’s a hidden feature difference beyond the form factors.

HomeView speaker system is much more powerful on model with domed base

If you’re trying to decide which HomeView form factor to buy, there’s a key detail you should know about.

Beyond the obvious design differences between the model with a domed base—‘HomeView’—and the one designed for your wall—‘HomeView (Wall Mounted)’—there’s a disparity in capabilities too.

The standard HomeView has a much more powerful speaker system built in. Here are Apple’s descriptions of each speaker setup:

HomeView delivers room-filling sound with support for Spatial Audio, making it a great way to enjoy music and podcasts at home. Its custom-engineered acoustic system combines a down-firing woofer and two full-range drivers to produce deep bass and crisp highs. Powered by the A18 chip and built-in sensors, computational audio continuously optimizes the loudness and bass response at any volume. 

HomeView (Wall Mounted) brings full, balanced sound with two custom drivers and computational audio tuned specifically for on-wall placement, along with support for Spatial Audio.

	

Echoing this, Apple’s technical specs page confirms both models have two custom full-range drivers, but the HomeView with domed base adds:

Custom down-firing woofer

Dual force-cancelling passive radiators

Essentially, if you want the best sound experience from your HomeView, you’ll want to buy the standard model.

But if audio quality isn’t as important to you, the wall-mounted version will probably get the job done. It still has built-in speakers, but it won’t deliver the same performance and thus isn’t as well-suited for everyday music playback.

Does the difference in audio quality change your HomeView purchase decision at all? Let us know in the comments.

title: Waymo Puts Toronto on the Map for Its Robotaxis
snippet: Training of the Waymo robotaxis will begin in the coming days, but you won’t be able to book a ride till 2028.
fullText:
Waymo is bringing its autonomous ride services across the border to Canada for the first time. 

The company said in a blog post on Friday that its robotaxis will be available for you to book rides in the app in the Toronto area in 2028. It will start with a limited number of its mainstay Jaguar I-Pace electric SUVs, and will add more over time. 

But if you’re in Toronto, you can expect to see Waymo cars, driven by humans, in the coming days as the company maps local street networks and acclimates its autonomous technology to traffic patterns and driving conditions. 

		

			

Waymo will test in select Toronto neighborhoods, including Liberty Village, St. Lawrence Market and Yorkdale. It has also built a sixth-generation Waymo Driver autonomous driving system to navigate diverse environments, including the extreme winter weather Toronto faces in the colder months. A Waymo representative did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The company is also partnering with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management for vehicle maintenance, validation driving and customer service.

Waymo launched its fully autonomous ride service featuring electric vehicles in 2018. The ride service is currently available in the US in places including Miami, Phoenix and the San Francisco Bay Area. Earlier this year, Denver, San Diego, Las Vegas and Tampa were added to the list of available cities.

Sign-ups to ride with Waymo in Toronto and track the progress of the Canadian launch are now open on Waymo’s website.

When installing macOS 27 (Golden Gate), Rosetta is automatically removed. If you manage a fleet with any legacy Intel-only software still in use, you need a plan in place before your users start experiencing issues. Here is what I’m doing, and I have some thoughts on vendors who are waiting until the last minute to deploy Apple Silicon-native tools.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

The silent failure problem

One thing I need to clarify is that macOS 27 removes it, but macOS 28 will no longer support it. For traditional apps, macOS 27 will prompt the user to reinstall it with an easy-to-follow GUI prompt. That’s actually the workable scenario, because at least the user knows something is wrong, and macOS reinstalls it. The tools I’m worried about are the ones that won’t do that. I have a handful of menu bar utilities from vendors who haven’t shipped a native Apple Silicon build yet, and in my testing this summer, they are just silently failing. There’s no error prompt. It just fails to work. That makes auditing your fleet before macOS 27 rolls out more important than it might seem at first glance.

What I’m doing in my device management system

My short-term fix is to automatically push a Rosetta reinstallation script to every Mac that joins my macOS 27 Dynamic Device Group. In Mosyle, the setup is really straightforward. You create a new script profile, name it something obvious like “Rosetta Install macOS 27,” and enter the following command in the script tab:

softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license

Under Execution Settings, pick your preferred trigger, then assign the profile to your macOS 27 Dynamic Device Group and save. When a device appears in that group, Mosyle automatically pushes the script, and Rosetta (hopefully) gets installed before the user ever runs into a problem. It’s not a permanent fix, but it buys time while I work on the real solution: getting vendors to ship native builds.

On the vendors

I want to be direct about this. Apple Silicon shipped in late 2020. We are now in late 2026. Any vendor still telling customers that a native Apple Silicon build is “on the roadmap” before Rosetta stops working in macOS 28 has had five-plus years to solve this problem and has chosen not to. That is not a resource issue or a technical challenge at this point. It is a prioritization choice, and one that falls squarely on the IT teams managing their software. Even if these vendors ship Apple Silicon-native versions before macOS 28, the shipping delay makes me question their commitment to macOS.

Wrap up

If you haven’t audited your fleet for Rosetta-dependent software yet, do it now while there’s still time to either push a script workaround or have the harder vendor conversations before users start running into problems. Most enterprise fleets are likely doing a 90 day block on Golden Gate for final testing/QA, so now is the time to work on your final plan. The script fix in Mosyle takes about five minutes to set up. Vendor conversations will take longer, and migrating to new solutions will take a bit longer.

title: Tesla Roadster Fires Up SpaceX Tech for ‘Flying Car’ Demo
snippet: I’m no rocket scientist, but I’m not sure the vehicle on display was a fully functional car that a human can drive.
fullText:
On Thursday night in Texas, Tesla unveiled the long-awaited, production-intent second-generation of its Roadster electric sports car, showcasing a wild array of unbelievable party tricks, including driving upside down, performing aerial barrel rolls and hopping over other cars with the aid of SpaceX thruster and suction technology. 

Surprisingly, the angular coupe that rolled onto the stage looked almost nothing like the curvaceous concept car that the automaker revealed almost nine years ago. Back in 2017, Tesla’s would-be halo car targeted a 1.9-second 0-60 time, 620 miles of range and production in 2020. That deadline came and went, and the Roadster was delayed multiple times as Tesla CEO Elon Musk shifted his focus from robotics to robotaxis to politics. The new-look Roadster seems to be built as a showcase of the combined might of the cross-owned, Musk-helmed tech giants: Tesla, xAI and SpaceX.

‘This car sucks’

The demonstration opened with the new Roadster showcasing its angular Cybertruck-inspired design from an unconventional angle: by driving up a massive ramp and onto a wall where it was held vertically by suction fans. Tesla Vice President of Engineering Lars Moravy, on stage at the event, later said the underbody system can generate up to 2Gs of suction, allowing the EV to stick to the road — and apparently walls as well. 

		

			

“I mean, this car really sucks,” Musk added. “This car could suck the chrome off a trailer hitch. It could suck a tennis ball through a hose pipe.”

What a class act.

Next, the Roadster backed up, stopped and accelerated toward the C-shaped ramp again, driving upside down momentarily before launching into the air, performing a barrel roll with the aid of 10 SpaceX cold gas thrusters located under and around the vehicle’s body — the same tech used to adjust the position and attitude of satellites and craft in zero-g space. As the night continued, the Roadster was shown hopping over a lineup of Tesla vehicles while performing another barrel roll, its thrusters causing the EV to pivot in midair and cushion its landing.

The Tesla Roadster at the event was likely a stripped-down, remotely controlled mule.Tesla

I’m no rocket scientist, but I’m not sure the vehicle on display was a fully functional car that a human can drive. The windows appeared completely opaque, hinting at no cockpit, and the aerobatics seemed implausible for a long-range EV, often laden with hundreds of pounds of battery. More likely, this was a stripped-down, remote-controlled mule with just enough battery onboard to complete the demo, and it’s highly unlikely that we’ll see a true production flying car equipped with this tech.

2028 production target

Aside from the promise of pirouetting over traffic, the Tesla Roadster’s on-road performance is said to be impressive. 

In addition to the promised ability to corner at more than 2 g of lateral acceleration, the company says the electric sports car will complete a 0-60 mph sprint in 1 second, or 0.81 second with the aid of the SpaceX thrusters. The automaker says the top “Rocket” spec will be a limited-edition, “invite-only” model not available to the public. (I’d wager these “flying cars” wouldn’t exactly be street-legal and would be limited to closed-course shenanigans.) All of these figures are Tesla’s own and have yet to be independently confirmed.

Musk said the car would be offered in three trim levels, including the Rocket Roadster, and that Tesla is aiming for a production target sometime in 2028. Tesla did not reveal final prices, updated range estimates or any other relevant details, but reservations have opened at a hefty $50,000 apiece on the Roadster reservation page.

title: TikTok permanently bans ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account
snippet: A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

1:55 PM PDT · October 17, 2026

Image Credits:Tierney L. Cross/The Washington Post/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms, with TikTok banning the film’s advertising account.

According to a story in The Hollywood Reporter, the documentary’s distributor Bleecker Street was recently notified by TikTok that the account had received a “permanent suspension” due to its political content. TechCrunch has reached out to TikTok for comment.

Ads promoting the trailer for “Musk” — directed by Oscar-winner filmmaker Alex Gibney — were  initially rejected by Meta and YouTube as well, though those platforms eventually allowed the ad, with Meta blaming the rejection on “an error.” Gibney recently confirmed that the film’s international distributor Universal had wavered in its plans to release “Musk,” though it’s now moving forward.

X, which Musk owns, has refused to carry ads for “Musk.” TikTok’s U.S. operations are partly owned by Larry Ellison — who, like Musk, has been a notable supporter of President Donald Trump.

“Musk” opened in just four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more broadly. Next year, it’s supposed to stream on HBO — now part of Paramount/Skydance and led by Ellison’s son David.

Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film’s social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, was informed Friday afternoon that a “permanent suspension” was imminent. Bleecker Street has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge.

While TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, part owner Larry Ellison appears in the film via a text message offering to help Musk fund his Twitter purchase.

Last month, YouTube, Meta, X, and TikTok all faced backlash for rejecting ads for the film. YouTube and Meta quickly reversed course, calling it an “error.” However, TikTok and X have refused to change their stance, and neither platform has allowed paid advertisements for the film.

Banning the documentary’s account, however, marks a serious escalation, and one laced with a dash of irony — shortly before the account was removed, it posted that people should see the movie “before it gets shut down.”

title: In ‘You Can See Everything,’ Elizabeth Holmes meets her equal in comedian Nathan Fielder
snippet: Nathan Fielder's documentary about disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes has created a constellation of colliding personas that interrogate the very nature of authenticity.
fullText:
“Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes.

One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is.

“I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.”

No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral, Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble.

“If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes.

“It was real.”

“I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.”

We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered.

Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore.

In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas.

“The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.”

[The rest of this review contains spoilers.]

Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up.

And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article.

At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “The Dropout” because “they’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.”

She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos.

Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does.

Amanda Seyfried portrays Elizabeth Holmes in “The Dropout.”Image Credits:Beth Dubber/Hulu

Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.”

Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner in crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries.

In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth. Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there.

The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas. Though it’s a nonfiction documentary, it’s clear that everyone involved is, to some extent, also performing for the cameras. How could they not? Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year.

Meanwhile, Evans behaves in such an unfathomably egregious manner that he may even be intentionally playing the villain to drum up sympathy for his reviled wife.

Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence. This documentary will not sway anyone to believe that his wife is being wrongly held in federal custody. But Evans makes himself appear so appallingly unlikable that some viewers may leave the theater feeling bad for Holmes, seeing her as a victim and allowing her to double down on another persona she adopted while on trial: a harmless, docile woman who was manipulated by her ex-partner to obliviously tell a cascade of increasingly harmful lies.

Once Holmes is in jail, Fielder is not allowed to bring recording devices when he visits her, so he tries to write a script of their conversations from memory, struggling to accurately re-create the nuances of a conversation where every last word carries immense meaning. With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery.

In character as Holmes, Seyfried says, “People think Amanda’s show is a documentary. I get treated worse [in prison] because of how she portrayed me.”

As she reads the lines, Seyfried breaks character.

“I didn’t do that,” the actress says. “She did that to herself.”

title: OnePlus 16 goes official with 9,000 mAh battery, and it just makes me sad
snippet: The OnePlus 16 is official this week and looks beastly – too bad most of the world won’t be able to buy it. more…
fullText:
The OnePlus 16 is official this week and looks beastly – too bad most of the world won’t be able to buy it.

It was always going to sting when OnePlus launched its next flagship after pulling out of global markets, but it’s especially rough when it’s actually a pretty big improvement over the OnePlus 15. 

Announced earlier this week in China, the OnePlus 16 is packing some serious power.

6.78-inch 2772×1272 185Hz OLED display

Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

Up to 16GB RAM

Up to 1TB storage

9,000 mAh battery (100W/80W wired & wireless charging)

200MP main camera, 50MP ultrawide, 50MP 3x telephoto, 50MP front-facing

The battery figure alone is staggering, as the OnePlus 15 was already turning heads with its 7,300 mAh power pack. GSMArena points out that the OnePlus 16’s 185Hz display is limited to 165Hz generally, but opens up the full refresh rate when playing games. 

Open sales of OnePlus 16 in China start on October 31 with pricing starting at CNY 5,999 – around $900 USD. 

But, with OnePlus having pulled out or scaled back in effectively every other global market, don’t expect this one to make its debut elsewhere.

title: iPhone 18 Pro one month later: These features keep impressing me
snippet: I’ve had the iPhone 18 Pro for about a month now, and during that time three main features have consistently impressed me. more…
fullText:
I’ve had the iPhone 18 Pro for about a month now, and during that time three main features have consistently impressed me.

#1: Battery life

When Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro, it compared its battery life to that of the iPhone 17 Pro Max—a model universally praised for its impressive runtime.

After a month of use, iPhone 18 Pro’s battery truly is top-tier. I never even think about charging it during the day, and at the end of almost every day I have about 60% battery left.

I can’t even imagine what I’d end the day with if I had the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max. Suffice to say, Apple’s battery upgrades this year are excellent, and anyone with an older model iPhone should be very happy regardless of which Pro size you choose.

#2: Main camera upgrades

Apple makes the iPhone’s cameras better every year. But it’s actually not too often that the Main camera improves substantially. In the last couple years, for example, Apple has focused more on upgrading the Telephoto, Ultra Wide, and Front cameras.

But iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera with variable aperture is the star this year, and I’ve been loving it.

I don’t have professional photography training, so the addition of pro controls isn’t appealing to me. And I never manually change apertures with the camera. But just using the ‘Auto’ setting, I keep taking photos that look especially great to me. Most of the time they’re  ƒ/1.48, with some ƒ/1.8 thrown in too. And while I don’t have the expertise to describe why they look so good to me, I’ll just say I’ve been very happy with the camera.

#3: Vapor chamber cooling

I use my iPhone outdoors a lot, on frequently sunny days, and iPhone 18 Pro’s vapor chamber has been a welcome upgrade in keeping the iPhone usable.

Previous iPhone models would often struggle out in the elements, especially on warm, bright days. This proved especially frustrating when I was trying to capture a special moment with the Camera app and my warm iPhone was too sluggish to snap the photo.

With iPhone 18 Pro, while it still occasionally gets slightly warm, I’ve never noticed a delay in performance as a result. Instead, the vapor chamber keeps everything cool enough to deliver the iPhone experience I expect.

The Fitbit Air is finally getting another band option that isn’t fabric or polyurethane. Instead, the Metal Mesh band might actually take the Fitbit Air up a notch.

Band selection for the Fitbit Air has been limited. The Elevated Modern band and Performance Loop options are good, but they lack a little flair. The Fitbit Air needed another band option to take advantage of just how easy it is to swap styles.

The Metal Mesh band fills that gap. It comes in Polished Silver and Champagne Gold with the intent of matching your existing jewelry. The look lets the wearable blend in with an elevated outfit, even if the Performance Loop band does a good job fitting most looks.

Google says the Metal Mesh band for the Fitbit Air will be priced at $69.99. You’ll also be able to buy the Fitbit Air with the Metal Mesh band and the Performance Loop band for $149.99 as a bundle, but it only comes in gold. That’s $20 more than the special editions, like the Steph Curry band and the Pokémon Sleep band, but it comes with two bands instead of a single option.

	

Packed into the band announcement, Google detailed a couple more feature additions to the Fitbit Air, regardless of band choice.

Google announced Health Guardian features that analyze your overall health picture. For Google Health Premium users who set up blood pressure and insulin resistance trends in the app, a report will be available each month to guide lifestyle adjustments. This may give the AI Health Coach some more usability for the average Fitbit user.

Google also notes that automatic activity tracking is getting an overhaul. According to the new post, Google claims the improvements will result in “more intelligent, accurate, and reliable” tracking.

Tracks more activities: We expanded the number of activities your Fitbit tracker or Pixel Watch can detect from 10 to more than 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket and team sports.

Uses more context: Powered by contextual reasoning, Google Health factors in critical context — including your workout routines, historical data, manual edits, and, with permission, your location — to deliver nearly 2x more accurate detections and cut missed workouts by more than half. 7

Logs workouts automatically: Workouts that meet your minimum duration threshold (15 minutes by default) with a sustained elevated heart rate are automatically logged, and a summary is sent to your mobile app, typically within 30 minutes.

Learns your patterns: When you confirm or edit an activity, you’re improving a feature that learns your unique patterns and uses them to refine its predictions.

These updates are planned for “later this month.” This comes as the company recently announced a more expensive $179 tracker called the Fitbit Edge. Unlike the Fitbit Air, this model has a screen carrying Google’s Material You design language.

As for the new Metal Mesh bands, Google has them available for pre-order on its website and at Target. It looks like the new bands should ship later this month.

title: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
snippet: The biggest change about Ember's new mug is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature.
fullText:
With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip.

Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades.

The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click.

Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate.

It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app. 

That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach.

If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings.

Image Credits:Ember

The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.)

The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149.

The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green.

Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out.

The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

fullText:
Apple’s debut in the foldable market was always going to have an impact on Android foldables, with many brands having been optimistic that it would have a positive ripple effect. For Samsung, that appears to be true, as the company says that interest in its Galaxy Z Fold 8 remains significantly higher following the iPhone Duo’s announcement.

Speaking to Forbes, Samsung’s UK VP over mobile said that demand for Galaxy Z Fold 8 has risen following the debut of iPhone Duo, with search interest even higher — apparently up by 300%.

Samsung’s foldable momentum is undeniable… Customer demand for the Galaxy Z Fold8 family has increased 16% since launch, and with a 300% increase in active Google searches for Samsung foldables in the last month alone, our market leadership is stronger than ever.

It’s not hard to imagine why this might be the case.

Apple’s massive and loyal fanbase means that the launch of iPhone Duo put foldables under the spotlight for effectively the first time for a lot of potential buyers, so it only makes sense that at least a portion of those users are curious to see what else is out there. Samsung’s lower prices and more refined design might also have a few folks interested enough to give the alternative a shot.

	

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is currently available for $1,699 on Amazon, $300 less than iPhone Duo, while Samsung.com is offering the Fold 8 for even less than that, with a special discount on the 1TB trim that offers the device for just $50 more than Apple’s base 256GB model.

title: If a Chromebook wasn’t for you, Googlebook isn’t either
snippet: Let’s not pretend; if you weren’t sold on a Chromebook, Googlebook isn’t for you either. more…
fullText:
Let’s not pretend; if you weren’t sold on a Chromebook, Googlebook isn’t for you either.

In our review of Googlebook as a platform, Abner Li explains how this platform sets a foundation for a potentially fascinating future. But, even from that viewpoint, it’s hard to ignore the shortcomings. Between the app gap and plenty of overlooked mistakes throughout the OS, Googlebook is far from a “finished” product.

In many ways, it continues to resemble what it’s replacing, ChromeOS, and that’s not going to leave the best impression for everyone.

Chromebook launched to a market starved of capable and reliable cheap laptops, and at a time where even higher-end machines were inherently compromised. Better battery life, no virus protection, simpler setup, price, take your pick, a Chromebook was a genuinely good choice for quite a while. But, as time went on, that math started to shift away from Google’s favor. I’d argue that it’s harder to find a bad laptop than it is a good one now, and there are good options on every price point, whether you’re looking at Windows or a MacBook. There’s an abundance of fully-capable Windows machines with long battery life and plenty of power, and frankly, the MacBook Air is $1,099.

	

With that in mind, Googlebook’s inherent similarities to ChromeOS betray any progress it might have made.

Under the hood, the new Android base is a much better foundation for the years to come. On the surface, where the users are, Googlebook hasn’t addressed any of the issues ChromeOS was dealing with, at least from a functional level. Apps are the biggest problem, as everything from mainstays to the niche library of apps are a shell on Googlebook of what they are on Windows and macOS. Unless you’re heavily using the web or Android apps for everything you do, you’re going to run into times where Googlebook is simply incapable of doing the things you want. And that even goes for Google’s own product offerings. Within the past week Google announced a new app that could combine voice recordings, shorthand notes, and local AI processing to build out detailed notes of a meeting or presentation. It’s a really useful and fun idea, but you literally cannot use it on Googlebook — it’s exclusive to Mac. 

Even the whole “this is a laptop for Android users” schtick doesn’t hold any water. These features are nonexistent at launch for most users, and ChromeOS had the vast majority of these anyway. 

	

Put simply, Googlebook isn’t a reset from ChromeOS. It’s not catching up to the competition. It’s the same old problems (plus a few new ones) in an admittedly much faster and more polished new chassis. The future might tell a different story but, at least for now, Googlebook is not for you if a Chromebook wasn’t.

title: Apple SVP Greg Joswiak: ‘We don’t feel threatened’ by OpenAI hardware plans
snippet: Today in a new story at TIME, the publication interviewed CEO John Ternus but also spoke to Greg “Joz” Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing, who addressed the “lunatic fringe” of AI in Silicon Valley, hardware threats from OpenAI, and more. more…
fullText:
Today in a new story at TIME, the publication interviewed CEO John Ternus but also spoke to Greg “Joz” Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing, who addressed the “lunatic fringe” of AI in Silicon Valley, hardware threats from OpenAI, and more.

Here’s what Greg Joswiak said about Apple’s AI strategy, threats from OpenAI, more

TIME picked the iPhone Duo as one of 2026’s best inventions and interviewed CEO John Ternus plus a few other Apple execs for the story.

One of those other interviewees, SVP of Worldwide Marketing Greg Joswiak, addressed Apple’s AI strategy, OpenAI hardware efforts, and more.

When asked about the ChatGPT maker’s hardware plans, Joswiak said: “We don’t feel threatened. The fact that we can do the integration that we can means we can create just a better experience than anybody else.” 

Apple’s integration of hardware, software, and services has long been central to the company’s product ethos. And it clearly believes those ecosystem strengths will be a strong defense against new competitors.

	

Joswiak also implies that perhaps OpenAI’s products won’t have as broad appeal as Apple devices do. From the story’s very next paragraph:

Joswiak adds that Apple isn’t making products for the die-hard AI believers chasing superintelligence. “We love them, and they can use it too, but that’s not our target,” he says. “It’s how to make it better for everyday people.”

This sort of split between the average person and the AI enthusiast is also highlighted by Joswiak elsewhere in the interview. Andrew Chow writes:

While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years…But Ternus and other Apple executives say they aren’t concerned. In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley’s “lunatic fringe,” as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it.

Joswiak doesn’t define this “lunatic fringe,” but by contrasting it with Apple’s own efforts to “help ordinary people,” he’s making a clear distinction.

title: John Ternus talks iPhone Duo, ‘cheap and crappy’ foldables in new interview
snippet: TIME has just published its list of the best inventions of 2026, and iPhone Duo made the list with John Ternus featured on the magazine cover. Here’s what Ternus said in his interview with TIME. more…
fullText:
TIME has just published its list of the best inventions of 2026, and iPhone Duo made the list with John Ternus featured on the magazine cover. Here’s what Ternus said in his interview with TIME.

John Ternus on iPhone Duo origins, delay to market, more

John Ternus sat down with TIME for a wide-ranging interview centered on iPhone Duo, but also covering a variety of other topics, including AI.

Regarding the iPhone Duo, which is hitting the market nearly a decade after other foldables, Ternus was involved in early foldable work at Apple all the way back in 2011.

In 2011, when many people still carried around flip phones, Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, exploring what kind of batteries and circuit boards might be needed for such an idea. “It felt clear that we were going to eventually get to a place where OLED displays were going to be flexible,” Ternus says.

Ternus wasn’t a fan of early attempts at foldables from other companies in the 2010s. He says, “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy.”

The drive to achieve a foldable unlike its competitors is evidenced by a story from Richard Dinh, Apple’s VP of Product Design.

Along the way, Ternus encouraged the team to invest more time and effort in the project, even as other foldables beat them to market. Dinh says that at one point, he asked Ternus whether his team should proceed with a top surface material similar to those of its competitors, which Dinh felt had flaws but was potentially good enough.

“And he was like, ‘Look, Rich, you’ll know when it’s the right thing.’ And that gave us the confidence to really push the boundaries on innovation and manufacturing, and fly worldwide to connect our suppliers together and come up with the nanotexture [a surface technology],” Dinh says. The result—a surface made from a custom polymer and built atop a hinge with more than 100 tiny interior precision components—has impressed its first users, who have said they can barely detect a crease at all.

	

The story also mentions that Ternus “has devoted much of his early tenure as CEO to obsessing over design, spending multiple days a week in the studio with the industrial-design and human-interface teams.” This echoes previous Bloomberg reporting around Ternus’s early priorities.

Other topics Ternus addresses in the interview include:

Apple Intelligence’s reliance on Gemini technology: “There’s not really a goal that we have to make every single thing in a product. We make the things where we can really bring differentiation.”

Siri AI’s unique advantages: “Everything in your life is on your phone. With Siri AI, you can leverage all that information to do things, learn things, and figure out things in a way that nobody else can do.”

Not sleeping much before September event: “I was on such a moment of adrenaline and caffeine and excitement for the day.”

title: Apple lists unreleased iPad mini accessory ahead of rumored launch
snippet: While Apple is rumored to be gearing up to introduce an OLED iPad mini later this month, an oversight on the company’s French site might have just confirmed the product’s existence. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
While Apple is rumored to be gearing up to introduce an OLED iPad mini later this month, an oversight on the company’s French site might have just confirmed the product’s existence. Here are the details.

Next-gen iPad mini likely to get a new Smart Folio

As spotted by MacRumors, Apple’s French regulatory website currently lists a Smart Folio for iPad mini with the model number A3632, which doesn’t correspond to any existing products.

The regulatory document is dated September 8, 2026, although it’s unclear when Apple actually added the listing to its website.

Compared with the Smart Folio for iPad mini (6th generation), whose regulatory document is dated December 22, 2022, the unreleased accessory has some notable differences.

According to Apple’s documentation, the new Smart Folio contains at least 3% recycled materials, compared with a minimum of 9% in the current model. It also contains at least 6,610 milligrams of rare earth elements, compared with 3,947 milligrams in the previous version, which could indicate changes to the magnets used to attach the cover to the iPad.

While these figures don’t reveal anything specific about the accessory’s design, the fact that Apple has assigned it a new model number suggests that changes may be coming.

For context, the sixth- and seventh-generation iPad mini models are compatible with the same Smart Folio, so a new accessory could indicate that the upcoming model will feature physical changes that affect case compatibility.

The next-gen iPad mini is rumored to feature an OLED display, Apple’s A20 Pro chip, thinner bezels, a relocated front-facing camera, and a redesigned speaker system. Bloomberg has also reported that Apple is working on a more water-resistant design, while recent rumors suggest the device could cost considerably more than its predecessor.

There are currently conflicting reports on whether the new iPad mini will retain a 60Hz refresh rate or gain support for 120Hz ProMotion.

While previous reports had left the possibility of ProMotion open, leaker yeux1122 recently reiterated that the device will be limited to a 60Hz OLED display.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has indeed tested both options, but he hasn’t been able to confirm which one the company ultimately chose.

title: Samsung rolling out major Health update with Sleep & Running coach, meal scanning
snippet: The Samsung Health app is getting a pretty major update this week with support for new coaches for sleep and running, as well as support for scanning meals to track calories and macros. more…
fullText:
The Samsung Health app is getting a pretty major update this week with support for new coaches for sleep and running, as well as support for scanning meals to track calories and macros.

Starting with its new coaches, Samsung Health will now offer tips and help build checklists to improve their sleep quality, as well as getting analysis on their sleep tracking data (from Galaxy Watch or Ring) to identify trends. 

Samsung explains:

Informed by principles of behavioral sleep science, the program gives users daily habit checklists and sleep tips — supporting users in building routines around everyday wellness, such as avoiding screens an hour before bed, skipping late caffeine and stretching outdoors after waking up.

Users can also enjoy more intuitive and detailed analysis reports. The new pentagon-shaped Sleep Balance graph consolidates five key aspects of sleep indicators —sleep time, sleep regularity, awake time during the night, sleep satisfaction, and Energy Score— to provide an at-a-glance view of sleep trends and areas that may warrant attention, based on data collected or inputted through sleep coaching.

Beyond that, Samsung Health’s Running Coach is also getting upgrades with new training levels, a social media sharing feature, and deeper integration with Strava. This includes importing Strava running, trail, and cycling routes into Samsung Health.

	

The other big addition here, at least for users in the US, is “Scan Meal.”

This new beta feature allows users to take a photo of their meal and have Samsung Health leverage AI resources to identify the food and the serving size and provide an estimate of calories and macros. This isn’t some wild new idea – Google Health does the same – but it’s certainly convenient if you’re already invested in Samsung Health. This also comes with a new “Diet Score” feature that helps you adjust your diet to support goals such as eating vegetables, upping protein, or limiting sugar and processed foods.

Samsung says:

Using data inputted into the feature, users also receive a Diet Score, calculated through a Samsung nutrition assessment model. Similar to the Sleep and Energy Scores, which utilize on-device and cloud-based algorithms to analyze users’ activity data, the Diet Score is categorized into four tiers — Needs Attention, Fair, Good, and Excellent — to provide users with a general snapshot of certain aspects of their eating habits. The diet data that is input is analyzed through seven focused dimensions, spanning food groups and beverage and food habits, guiding users to manage their food intake to support diet choices like eating vegetables and proteins while limiting sugar-sweetened beverages and ultra-processed foods.

These updates are rolling out now.

fullText:
Language that experts say allowed the scraping of news sites to train its AI has been removed from Meta’s terms.

Language that experts say allowed the scraping of news sites to train its AI has been removed from Meta’s terms.

by  Terrence O'Brien

Oct 17, 2026, 3:04 PM UTC

Illustration by Nick Barclay / The Verge

Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page:

… Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

Many, including Neiman Lab and James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, interpreted it as an attempt to give Meta the right to use content scraped from sites to train its AI products for free and supersede blocking instructions in a site’s robots.txt file.

Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, and spokesperson Daniel Roberts pushed back, saying that “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false.” Today’s update to its terms and a new statement go further, removing the controversial language entirely. Roberts said in a follow-up statement to The Verge this morning:

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

title: HomePod is about to get free upgrade with these new features
snippet: Apple unveiled three new Home products this week: HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and a new Apple TV 4K. While there’s no new full-size HomePod launching, Apple did announce three features coming to the existing HomePod 2 via a free software update. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled three new Home products this week: HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and a new Apple TV 4K. While there’s no new full-size HomePod launching, Apple did announce three features coming to the existing HomePod 2 via a free software update.

#1: Sound Glow

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone, your HomePod will get the new Sound Glow feature that’s also coming to HomePod mini 2.

Per Apple’s webpage for HomePod (2nd generation): “with Sound Glow, the top of your HomePod lights up with colors that match your album artwork, pulsing in tune with the music.”

The HomePod mini 2 announcement adds more details, which hopefully will be the same on the larger HomePod:

With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod mini transforms into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble. The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere.

#2: Default speaker for Mac

Apple has long let you use a HomePod as a speaker for your Mac via AirPlay. But soon, you’ll be able to set HomePod as the default Mac speaker for a more seamless, reliable connection.

Like Sound Glow, Apple announced this feature for HomePod mini 2, but its fine print says:

Compatible with HomePod mini 2 and HomePod (2nd generation) with support on all Mac desktops and laptops with Wi-Fi 6E or later.

So if you want to upgrade your Mac speaker setup with the HomePod, or a stereo pair of HomePods, that will soon be easier than ever.

#3: Surround sound with four HomePods and Apple TV 4K

If you want the best, all-Apple home theater experience, a new surround sound feature for HomePod and Apple TV 4K will deliver that.

Exclusive to the new Apple TV 4K (4th gen), users can set up four HomePods—two as front speakers, two as rear—for a more immersive audio experience.

From Apple’s press release:

Home theater surround sound requires four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers in matching pairs (front and rear), paired with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) running the latest operating system software.

Apple hasn’t yet confirmed when these new features are launching on HomePod, but they’re expected to debut with iOS 27.2 and HomePod 27.2 later this month.

title: Google says fix for Android Auto’s missing signal icon is rolling out, and it actually is [U]
snippet: After weeks of back and forth, Google has officially confirmed a fix is rolling out for Android Auto’s missing signal icon. more…
fullText:
After weeks of back and forth, Google has officially confirmed a fix is rolling out for Android Auto’s missing signal icon.

The corner of every Android Auto display is meant to show your phone’s battery status, the time, a number of notifications, and your phone’s current cellular connection status.

The last one has been in rough shape.

While it hasn’t been consistent or fully widespread, many have found the cellular signal icon on Android Auto vanishing off and on for several weeks now. Recent updates have seemed to fix the issue for many, but now Google is confirming a fix has been made. In a comment on Reddit, a Google representative explains:

	

We’re aware of reports about the missing cellular signal, and we’re actually currently rolling out a fix that should hopefully address this issue! The fix isn’t widely available yet, though, so it may take some time to reach your device – if you want to receive it sooner, though, you can enroll in the Android Auto beta

The Android Auto beta program, notably, is full at the moment, but you can sideload updates (at your own risk). 

Android Auto 17.8 seems to deliver the fix, at least in part, and is now rolling out via the stable track.

Update 10/16: Google first confirmed the signal bar fix was rolling out earlier this month and, in the past day or two, it seems to have widely rolled out as more user reports have popped up, one of which points at Android Auto 17.8 as the reason. It’s still not back for everyone, it seems, but most users finally have this long-running bug fixed.

Images via Reddit (1, 2)

title: OpenAI agrees not to use alleged Apple trade secrets amid ongoing lawsuit
snippet: Bloomberg reports that during a hearing today, OpenAI voluntarily agreed not to use Apple’s alleged trade secrets while the legal battle between the two companies plays out. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that during a hearing today, OpenAI voluntarily agreed not to use Apple’s alleged trade secrets while the legal battle between the two companies plays out. Here are the details.

Apple scores second win in a row against OpenAI

Earlier today, OpenAI filed a new motion in the lawsuit in which Apple accuses the company of stealing trade secrets, alleging that a former employee who left OpenAI to return to Apple took more than 100 confidential files related to its unreleased hardware.

Soon after, the parties in the lawsuit appeared at a hearing where, as reported by Bloomberg, Judge Edward Davila indicated he was “highly likely” to grant Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction against OpenAI.

The short backstory on the injunction is the following: after Apple filed its trade secret misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products, the company also sought a preliminary injunction to prevent the defendants from accessing, using, or disclosing its confidential information while the case proceeds.

Apple also sought expedited discovery, requesting early access to internal documents, forensic evidence, and employee testimony to support its case for an injunction. Many of those requests were granted yesterday.

Back to today’s hearing, Judge Davila’s indication that he was “highly likely” to grant the injunction prompted OpenAI to voluntarily agree “not to use trade secrets that Apple Inc. claims were stolen,” as Bloomberg put it.

As part of the agreement established today, OpenAI also committed to collecting forensic images of devices from 14 employees “that may contain Apple’s confidential information,” says Bloomberg.

	

Judge Davila will have the authority to enforce the agreement, meaning OpenAI could face court-imposed sanctions if it fails to comply with its commitments.

However, the judge also reportedly pushed back against some of Apple’s demands, describing its request to inspect every device and repository that might contain its trade secrets as a “huge ask.”

In response, Apple’s attorney, John M. Desmarais, said the company would limit its inspections to a small group of former employees, adding that OpenAI doesn’t have “400 bad apples,” but rather “a few bad apples and know who they are.”

snippet: iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone, went up for pre-order today. Within minutes of pre-orders opening, however, estimated delivery dates started slipping all the way to next year. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone, went up for pre-order today. Within minutes of pre-orders opening, however, estimated delivery dates started slipping all the way to next year. 

The first iPhone Duo pre-orders are set to arrive on October 23, but only for the lucky people who placed their order in time. 

As of 8:30 a.m. ET, all iPhone Duo configurations are backordered until next year. All color and storage combinations show an estimated ship date of January 25. Some users are even seeing January 29 for their estimated shipping date.

This is a combination of strong demand and severely constrained supply for iPhone Duo. It’s impossible to know the exact balance between the two, though.  

	

Going into the launch, there were multiple reports suggesting iPhone Duo would be in short supply as Apple was still ramping up production. A report from Nikkei Asia last month said Apple was making just a few hundred iPhone Duo units per day, significantly behind the ramp of a normal iPhone launch. 

A quick glance on eBay reveals that there are already dozens of iPhone Duos available for pre-order from scalpers, asking as much as $5,200.

title: HomePod mini 2 vs HomePod mini: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple unveiled HomePod mini 2 yesterday (pre-order here), exactly six years after the first HomePod mini debuted. Here’s everything new in HomePod mini 2 compared to the original model. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled HomePod mini 2 yesterday (pre-order here), exactly six years after the first HomePod mini debuted. Here’s everything new in HomePod mini 2 compared to the original model.

Siri AI vs old Siri, plus microphone change

HomePod mini 2 is getting Siri AI support, bringing similar capabilities found in iOS 27 to Siri on your HomePod. This includes broad world knowledge, the ability to have rich, natural conversations, and music discovery upgrades. Additionally, personal context support means you can ask about a song you were recommended by a friend via Messages, get key information stored in your email, and more.

The original HomePod mini will not support Siri AI, leaving it stuck on the old Siri

Siri AI won’t be available right when HomePod mini 2 ships, but it’s expected to arrive as a software update next month.

Additionally, while it’s unclear if performance will be impacted, HomePod mini 2 has three far-field microphones for interacting with Siri, down from the four offered in HomePod mini.

New S10 chip vs S5

The original HomePod mini has a very dated S5 chip, which is unsurprising since it’s a 6-year-old device. But the new HomePod mini 2 runs a much more modern S10 chip.

S10 is the main reason HomePod mini 2 supports Siri AI while the original model doesn’t. Beyond that though, Apple doesn’t offer specific details on performance improvements to expect. However, it’s possible the audio experience will be upgraded. Per Apple’s press release:

Powered by the Apple S10 chip and advanced computational audio, [HomePod mini 2] analyzes music in real time to optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance.

Apple doesn’t explicitly say that the computational audio will be an improvement over what the previous model offered, but it’s certainly possible. We’ll have to wait for reviews to know for sure.

Sound Glow

Sound Glow is a new feature that makes the top of HomePod mini 2 come to life in response to the music it’s playing. Per Apple:

With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod mini transforms into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble. The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere.

Apple ecosystem features: Mac default speaker and Apple TV 4K surround sound

HomePod mini 2 includes two exclusive Apple ecosystem features not available on the original HomePod mini. One is for Mac users while the second involves the new Apple TV 4K.

Mac: HomePod mini 2 can be set as the default speaker for your Mac, either as a single speaker or a stereo pair. The original HomePod mini can only be used as a Mac speaker via AirPlay, so the connection isn’t as consistent and permanent.

Apple TV 4K: If you have the new fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, you can use a new HomePod surround sound feature for your TV. With surround sound, your Apple TV can use four HomePod mini 2 speakers for its audio output. You can also mix-and-match with the larger HomePod 2, for example with two HomePod 2 devices as front speakers and a HomePod mini 2 stereo pair as rear speakers.

Design updates: New colors and Siri animations

It goes without saying, but one key difference between HomePod mini 2 and the original model is the new lineup of colors.

HomePod mini 2: Blue, Green, Midnight, Pink, White

HomePod mini: Blue, Midnight, Orange, White, Yellow

Green and pink are the standout additions, but the new blue differs from the prior color too.

Additionally, HomePod mini 2 features a new design for animations on the top of the device. Essentially, Siri AI’s fresh color scheme replaces the old Siri appearance from the original HomePod mini.

Wireless connectivity upgrades

HomePod mini 2 comes with upgrades in both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth standards:

Strava expands strength training features

A few months ago, Strava announced an overhaul of its strength training experience, with a dedicated workout log for tracking sets, reps, and weights, automatic muscle maps, and more.

Today, the company unveiled new features that build on that, including coach-designed strength workouts that guide users through each exercise with animations, form tips, and information on the targeted muscle groups.

Rolling out to subscribers over the next few weeks, with a sample workout available to free users, the new experience walks athletes through workouts developed by experienced strength coaches with guided animations, and lets them track sets and reps live as they go. The company said today’s update also introduces new guided running workouts, with additional workout series planned before the end of the year.

And speaking of what’s coming, Strava says it’s working on a feature that will let users import strength workouts simply by uploading screenshots of training plans or notes containing sets and reps, “as well as a build-your-own workout feature.”

title: Apple Photos in iOS 27 upgrades one of my favorite features in a big way
snippet: Apple Photos is full of exciting updates in iOS 27, including for one of my favorite features in the app: iCloud Shared Albums. more…
fullText:
Apple Photos is full of exciting updates in iOS 27, including for one of my favorite features in the app: iCloud Shared Albums.

Apple’s Photos app is one of my most-used apps, as I suspect it is for many iPhone users. It’s where all of the photos and videos I capture live, plus screenshots, pictures shared by friends, and more.

But did you know that the Photos app also has a social media-style feature?

I’m not big on social media, but I do enjoy having a private, social-lite way to share memories with loved ones. And iCloud Shared Albums offers exactly that.

With iCloud Shared Albums, you can create an album that’s shared with only the people you choose. Anyone invited can add their own photos and videos, and you’ll get notified when they do. You can also ‘like’ shared photos and comment on them—just like a proper social network.

I’ve used and enjoyed Shared Albums for a long time, but the feature has felt in need of some upgrades. Fortunately, iOS 27 provides them.

In iOS 27, Shared Albums now support full-resolution photos and videos. That’s a huge item checked off my wish list.

Additionally, iOS 27 expands how you can react to a photo or video. Now you can use any emoji of your choosing as a reaction—you’re not limited to just ‘likes.’

For the first time, Android and Windows users can contribute to the album via the web. Previously, they could only view content shared by Apple users.

Apple has also made it easier to save shared photos with a tap. And you can set new participant permissions and optionally have your album expire at a later date.

These upgrades address all of the complaints I’ve previously had about Shared Albums. Combined with the other improvements in iOS 27, it’s a big year for Apple Photos.
